sections.title: Foreword

summary.text: Foreword: since NHWA's launch in 2017, and after a pandemic that disrupted health services, it is time to reflect on its progress. Focal points have been nominated by 90% of Member States, and standardized measurement, streamlined reporting and multi-stakeholder involvement have improved the availability and quality of health workforce data, informing evidence on shortages, ageing, migration, gender and subnational inequalities, the workforce's COVID-19 role, and reports such as the State of the World's Nursing and Midwifery. New World Health Assembly resolutions and initiatives since 2017 recognize the centrality of the health and care workforce. The revision keeps continuity with NHWA v1.0 and its core principles — systems strengthening, progressive implementation, multi-sectoral governance, diversified data sources — while adapting to new priority data needs and adding more examples of data use.

sections.extract: Several years have passed since the launch of the National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) in 2017. And following a global pandemic that disrupted healthcare services worldwide, it is an opportune time to reflect on the progress, priorities, gaps, and adaptations of the NHWA. sections.title: What is new?

summary.text: What is new in the second edition. The global health agenda changed after the COVID-19 pandemic, raising the need to strengthen the public health and emergency workforce, addressed by a 2022 Roadmap for the essential public health functions. A projected shortage of 10 million health and care workers by 2030 remains, and 181 countries, territories and areas now have a nominated NHWA focal point. New initiatives (the Working for Health programme, the Global Strategic Directions on Nursing and Midwifery, CHW guidance, the Global Health and Care Worker Compact) needed monitoring, and focal points and experts asked for fewer indicators. Version 2 therefore has four modules and 29 indicators: of version 1's 78 indicators, 62 were kept (often merged or turned into disaggregations or composite capacity indicators), 16 were dropped and 2 added — health workforce education and training capacity, and share of women in leadership role — retaining about 80% of version 1's information (Figure 1), with bridging tables to ease the transition. The section is inconsistent with itself here: Figure 1's per-module counts of dropped indicators (1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 2, 3, 1, 0, 0 across v1 modules 1–10) add up to 17, not the 16 dropped and 62 maintained stated in the text and the figure caption. The occupation list was revised and expanded along ISCO-08, and the focal-point data platform and public portal were updated.

sections.extract: This revision of the NHWA incorporates several aspects beyond data and indicators: the evolution of the global health agenda since 2017, new indicators needed and revision of existing indicators, the evolution of the occupations’ definitions, new tools and guidance. sections.title: Global context on health and care workers

summary.text: Global context on health and care workers: a health workforce of adequate size and skill mix is critical to UHC and the health-related SDGs, yet countries face challenges in education, deployment, performance and retention, and maldistribution limits access to services. The Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030, adopted in May 2016 by resolution WHA69.19, sets objectives including stronger HRH data, with milestones for 2020 and 2030, and stresses strengthened national HRH information systems. The High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth's report *Working for health and growth* set out 10 recommendations and a five-year action plan supported by ILO, OECD and WHO, leading to the joint Working for Health programme in 2017 and a call for harmonized health workforce data and metrics, which NHWA supports. COVID-19 (2020–2023) showed the workforce's central role: pulse surveys found shortages of health workers to be the most common cause of service disruptions and the biggest bottleneck to COVID-19 tools, underlining the need for a multisectoral workforce able to deliver the essential public health functions.

sections.extract: Global context on health and care workers A health workforce (HWF) of adequate size and skill mix is critical to the attainment of any population health goal. This includes the achievement of universal health coverage (UHC) (8) and the health-related targets of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). sections.title: Applications at the global level

summary.text: Applications at the global level: promoted by the High-Level Commission's action plan and the Global Strategy and supported by resolution WHA69.19, NHWA aims to standardize HRH information systems for interoperability so health workforce data can be exchanged and aggregated for decision-making. Since 2017, data availability and quality have improved greatly; as of April 2023, 181 countries, territories and areas have national focal points reporting annually on the NHWA data platform, and the public data portal has over 4,800 registered users. NHWA data underpin many knowledge products (Figure 2) and monitor global frameworks — the SDGs, UHC tracking, GPW13, the WHO Global Code of Practice on international recruitment, the nursing and midwifery strategic directions, the PHC measurement framework, Working for Health, the Health and Care Worker Compact, Immunization Agenda 2030 and the Global Oral Health Action Plan — and during COVID-19 were used to estimate health worker deaths, surge needs for vaccination and inequity in health worker vaccination.

sections.title: Applications at the regional level

summary.text: Applications at the regional level: country reporting and international comparison through NHWA support regional comparability, cross-country capacity building and knowledge exchange, regional HRH strategies and monitoring, and research on future workforce trends, and WHO regional offices have used NHWA to drive improved workforce monitoring across their countries.

sections.title: Applications at the national level

summary.text: Applications at the national level: NHWA indicators were chosen for policy relevance and can be adopted flexibly and modularly; countries select and prioritize modules to suit their needs and may mature towards covering all indicators, though full coverage is not a goal in itself. Implementation is progressive, with some benefits immediate and others longer term, and in five years countries have used it to set up multi-stakeholder governance, find data sources, strengthen HRH information systems and build a data-use culture. Box 1 lists national benefits — better understanding of workforce size, characteristics and distribution, evidence for policy, guidance for scaling education, intersectoral policy dialogue, cross-cutting investment and better planning — and the section closes with policy questions NHWA can inform, on availability and competence of the workforce, closing gaps through performance, retention, partnerships, education or in-migration, financing such policies, replacing exits, and incentives for underserved areas.

sections.extract: The NHWA indicators have been selected with clear policy relevance in mind, so that they can be used by any country according to its own specific needs. While designed to support a coherent framework for HWF policy analysis and design, the NHWA can be implemented and used in a flexible, modular way. sections.title: Definition

summary.text: Defines NHWA as a system by which countries progressively improve the availability, quality and use of health workforce data by monitoring a set of indicators, to support UHC, the SDGs and other health objectives.

sections.extract: The NHWA can be defined as – “a system by which countries progressively improve the availability, quality, and use of data on health workforce through monitoring of a set of indicators to support achievement of Universal Health Coverage, Sustainable Development Goals and other health objectives”.

sections.title: The underpinning framework

summary.text: The underpinning framework: NHWA is aligned with the health labour market framework for UHC (Figure 3), in which economy, population and societal drivers shape the education sector and labour market dynamics, with UHC and quality services as the outcome. It names four policy groups: on production (infrastructure, enrolment, student selection, teaching staff); on inflows and outflows (migration, attracting unemployed workers, bringing workers back); on maldistribution and inefficiencies (productivity, skill mix, retention in underserved areas); and to regulate the private sector (dual practice, training quality, service delivery). The first three follow an input–throughput–output sequence; the fourth spans the whole labour market. Annex 1 describes how NHWA was developed and revised.

sections.extract: The concept of the NHWA is closely aligned with the HLM framework for UHC (41) (Figure 3), which also takes a central place in the High-Level Commission’s report ‘Working for health and growth: investing in the health workforce’ (12). sections.title: A modular approach

summary.text: A modular approach: NHWA has 29 indicators in 4 modules (Figure 4), with Module 1 as the key starting point. Module 1, stock and flow, covers density, distribution by age, sex, sector and facility type, subnational distribution (for the Global Strategy milestone of halving inequalities in access to a health worker by 2030), foreign-trained and foreign-born workers (for halving dependency on foreign-trained professionals via the WHO Global Code), inflows, voluntary and involuntary outflows, and vacancies. Module 2, education, covers capacity, applications, enrolments and graduations, aligned with SDGs 4 and 5, plus accreditation and standards (milestone 4, by 2020). Module 3, finance and expenditure, maps workforce spending and remuneration including private earnings, informing investment and budget negotiation and SDGs 8 and 5. Module 4 covers labour regulations and policies (decent work, SDG 8), governance and leadership capacity through a central HRH unit, and HRH information system capacity to monitor planning metrics and global frameworks such as the WHO Global Code and the IHR. Every indicator has a standard descriptive page.

sections.title: Core principles of NHWA

summary.text: Core principles of NHWA: NHWA is a system-strengthening approach, not just an indicator list, keeping countries at the centre and letting them set the pace. An inclusive multi-sectoral, multi-stakeholder national governance mechanism is critical, helping to identify data sources, standardize collection, build partnerships, produce relevant analyses, drive data use and advocate for resources. Box 2 lists the principles: multi-stakeholder governance, system strengthening, progressive self-paced implementation, a parsimonious set of validated indicators or proxies, a country-owned process led by focal points, continuous updating from diverse existing sources with no primary data collection, and annual data release.

sections.extract: The NWHA is beyond just a list of indicators; it is a system-strengthening approach to improve the collection, collation, analysis and use of HWF data and enable evidence-informed HWF planning and policy-making. sections.title: Implementation and use of the NHWA

summary.text: Implementation and use of the NHWA: implementation is country-led, building on national systems and existing coordination mechanisms. WHO supports it with this Handbook, an implementation guide, an online reporting and visualization platform, and a public data portal publishing annually updated data as a global public good (Figure 5); regional offices and the Health Workforce Department (hrhstatistics@who.int) give direct support. NHWA has numeric and capability indicators (Part III), with policy-use examples in Part IV; the processes and units in indicator 4-02 (governance and leadership capacity) maximize policy use of the indicators, and indicator 4-05 addresses national capacity to monitor key planning and global-monitoring metrics.

sections.extract: Implementation and use of the NHWA Implementation of the NHWA The NHWA contains indicators with clear policy relevance across the entire spectrum of HWF priorities and those related to the HLM framework. The implementation of the NHWA is a country-led activity, building on national systems and using existing mechanisms to coordinate data-gathering for the evaluation of the HWF. sections.title: Methods for computing indicators

summary.text: Methods for computing indicators. Densities are health workers per 10,000 population, preferably using practising workers, otherwise professionally active, otherwise licensed workers (which may overestimate the workforce); global reporting uses UN World Population Prospects mid-year estimates. Distribution indicators must report all disaggregates and compute shares only from them, since mixing sources for numerator and total creates inconsistencies. Four indicators are composite scores: yes = 1, partial = 0.5, no = 0, scaled to 0–5 when at least 4 sub-indicators are reported, then classed as Sustainable (4.5–5), Well-developed (3.5–4.4), Moderate (2.5–3.4), Limited (1.5–2.4) or Nascent (<1.5), as in WHO SCORE; a worked example yields 3.75, and occupation-level answers are first averaged within a sub-indicator. Measurement is annual, as cross-sectional (31 December), cumulative (1 January–31 December) or cohort flows, with inflow rates using the end-of-year stock and outflow rates the start-of-year stock. Disaggregations written with a comma are independent and with 'and' joint, implemented progressively from the simplest; subnational levels follow the first or second administrative level. Financial data are converted to US$ at UN Treasury mid-year rates; focal points report only numerators for densities; occupations follow ISCO-08 (Annex 2), ideally at 4-digit level, and include personal care and health management and support workers; deviations from definitions should be reported with their methodology.

sections.extract: Computation of densities The density of HCWs is expressed per 10 000 population. It uses the stock of health workers divided by the size of the population multiplied by 10 000. sections.title: Synthesis of indicators

summary.text: Synthesis of indicators: tables giving, for each of the 29 NHWA v2 indicators, its number, short and full name, numerator, denominator and disaggregation. Module 1 (stock and flow) has 12: density per 10,000 (national and at the first subnational level), distribution by age group, sex, facility ownership, facility type, place of birth and place of training, annual inflow and outflow ratios (outflows by voluntary or involuntary exit), vacancy rate (funded full-time posts unfilled for at least twelve months over all funded posts) and distribution by full- or part-time contract; 'health workers' means all occupations in Annex 2, and population comes from UN World Population Prospects. Module 2 (education) has 7: training capacity per 10,000, applications to capacity, enrolments to applications, graduates to stock, programme duration, accreditation mechanisms, and standards for education and training with seven sub-indicators. Module 3 (finance) has 5: compensation expenditure, entry-level wages, education expenditure, expenditure per graduate and average tuition fee. Module 4 has 5: labour regulations and policies (12 sub-indicators, from working hours and minimum wage to attacks on health workers, mental well-being, CHW salaries and advanced nursing roles), governance and leadership capacity (5 sub-indicators), share of women in Ministry of Health senior management, IHR implementation capacity (rated None to Sustainable) and HRH information system capacity to monitor key metrics (9 sub-indicators).

sections.title: Bridging table

summary.text: Bridging table mapping each of the 78 NHWA version 1 indicators, across v1's ten modules (active stock; education and training; education regulation and accreditation; education finances; labour market flows; employment and working conditions; spending and remuneration; skill mix for models of care; governance and policies; information systems), to its version 2 indicator, with a status of maintained, merged, modified or dropped. Most stock indicators carry over to 1-01 to 1-08; the v1 regulation and accreditation standards, CPD and in-service training fold into 2-07; inflow and exit rates merge into 1-09 and 1-10; the working-hours, wage, social-protection, dual-practice, compulsory-service and attack-prevention regulations merge into 4-01, as does advanced nursing roles; facility-setting shares merge into 1-06 and specialist surgical and family medicine workforce into 1-01; the governance items merge into 4-02; IHR human resources becomes 4-04; and the HRHIS items, and the gender wage gap (modified), go into 4-05. Applications, admissions, drop-out and graduation rates are modified into 2-02 to 2-04. Seventeen rows are marked dropped, among them share of workers across health and social sectors, the master list of accredited institutions, student–educator ratio, total higher-education and in-service training expenditure, unemployment rate, standard working hours, attacks on the health-care system, total and ODA workforce expenditure, public-sector wage ceilings and applied epidemiology training.

sections.title: How to read indicator metadata

summary.text: How to read indicator metadata: each indicator has a metadata sheet; most are numeric ratios with a numerator and denominator, and some are capability indicators on the existence of regulations or processes. Every sheet follows the same order: indicator number (module, then indicator), abbreviated and full name (with possible values such as Yes/Partial/No for categorical indicators), numerator and denominator (numeric indicators only), disaggregation, definition and technical notes (including capability questions and answer options), glossary terms, data reporting frequency (annual or every three years), potential data sources at national level in decreasing order of relevance, and further information and links.

sections.extract: The indicators in the NHWA are presented as metadata sheets. The indicators are mostly numeric (quantitative), i.e. representing in numbers certain ratios with a numerator and denominator related to a HRH policy field. There are also capability indicators on the existence of certain regulations, processes, etc. reflecting the status of development of the HRH management system of a country. sections.title: – 01 Health worker density

summary.text: Lists the Module 1 indicators 1-02 to 1-12 and gives the metadata sheet for indicator 1-01, health worker density: active health workers (headcounts) per 10,000 population, disaggregated by occupation and by occupation and activity level (practising, professionally active, licensed to practise). The denominator is the UN World Population Prospects population, and WHO recalculates densities computed otherwise to keep them comparable. Reported annually, it feeds SDG 3.c.1 and 3.8.1, the WHO Global Code of Practice, the Global Strategy, Working for Health, SDNM, IA2030, SCORE, the PHC Measurement Framework, CHW guidance and the Global Oral Health Action Plan; sources include workforce registries, facility and HMIS/DHIS data, professional registers, labour force surveys, censuses and the UN Population Division.

sections.title: – 10 Annual outflows of health workers

summary.text: Metadata sheet for indicator 1-10, annual outflows of health workers: the share of active health workers who became inactive in the health labour market, using the active stock at the end of the previous year, disaggregated by occupation, by voluntary or involuntary exit and by sex. sections.title: Module 4: Working conditions, governance and leadership

summary.text: Opening of Module 4, Working conditions, governance and leadership: the module looks from three perspectives. The first indicator asks how well regulations and policies protect health workers; the second and third, from the national leadership side, look at mechanisms to coordinate the HRH agenda, including promoting women in leadership; the IHR indicator assesses workforce availability for emergency preparedness and response in line with the existing monitoring framework; and the last assesses capacity to report key metrics for frameworks mostly adopted by World Health Assembly resolutions. As national-level assessments covering all health and care workers, these indicators carry no disaggregation.

summary.text: Introduction to Part IV, Examples of how to use NHWA to inform policy development: it shows how NHWA indicators can be combined to inform policies for health and care workers. Each topic could warrant an in-depth health labour market analysis drawing on all indicators and further data, but once a policy is a national priority, selected indicators should be monitored regularly, with time trends showing whether the challenge is improving or new policies are needed; each topic is presented to help countries choose indicators for routine follow-up.

sections.title: HWF planning

summary.text: HWF planning: workforce planning is required to strengthen PHC and UHC, and a national workforce plan needs leadership and governance capacity, a solid situation analysis of gaps and trends, and coordination across sectors such as health, education, employment, finance, decentralization and social protection. In principle it uses most of the handbook's indicators, integrating stock, flows, migration, ageing, education and financing. A table picks six: health worker density (1-01) for current staffing, growth and fit with population need, annual inflows (1-09) and outflows (1-10) for workers entering and leaving the labour market, and governance and leadership capacity (4-02), IHR implementation capacity (4-04) and capacity to monitor key metrics (4-05) to judge whether the systems needed for planning are in place.

sections.extract: HWF planning is a requirement to strengthen PHC and UHC (9). The development of HWF national plan or other specific health plan can only be achieved if the leadership and governance capacity is available, building on a solid situation analysis that allows planners to identify gaps and trends. This includes the national coordination of multiple sectors (e.g, health, education, employment, finance, decentralization,

sections.title: Equity and subnational distribution

summary.text: Equity and subnational distribution: health and care workers are inequitably distributed globally and within countries, worst where density is already low, owing to factors such as salary differences driving migration, education not targeted at rural needs and no mechanisms to retain workers in rural and hard-to-reach areas. Planners need data on worker numbers and on demand from workload statistics, which facility-level studies using tools such as WISN can supply. Suggested indicators: density (1-01) for comparisons and trends across countries, income groups and subregions; subnational density of specialists (1-02) for gaps and redeployment; distribution by facility type (1-06); inflow trends of foreign-born or foreign-trained workers (1-09) for migration analysis; standards for social accountability and social determinants of health (2-07.1, 2-07.2) so education accounts for rural needs; entry-level wages (3-02) for earnings differences; and in-kind remuneration for rural retention (4-01.8).

sections.extract: Equity and subnational distribution There is globally a major inequity in the distribution of HCWs (3). This inequity is also present at subnational level of countries, and poses an even bigger problem in countries with already low density of health workers (25). sections.title: Retention

summary.text: Retention: reducing subnational inequity depends on retaining health and care workers in rural, remote and underserved areas. Retention problems show as a labour market mismatch in which workers are unemployed while jobs exist and posts stay vacant, and incentives are sometimes used to improve rural retention. Suggested indicators: density by occupation and activity level (1-01), contrasting the licensed with the practising workforce; vacancy rate (1-11) by area and occupation and its effect on facilities' PHC capacity; all labour regulation sub-indicators (4-01) on retention, dual practice, health and safety and working conditions; and subnational governance capacity (4-02), on whether decentralized HRH units can track careers, analyse current and future staffing needs, propose redeployment and retention strategies and support central policy-making and resource mobilization.

sections.extract: Retention The progress in reducing subnational inequities mentioned above relies on the capacity of countries to retain HCWs in rural, remote and other underserved areas. Retention challenges can be observed in the HLM when a misalignment exists with two phenomena occurring at the same time: unemployment of HCWs while several jobs are available and posts remain vacant. sections.title: Migration

summary.text: Migration: migration affects most countries, through reliance on foreign-trained workers or large-scale emigration. The WHO Global Code of Practice on international recruitment is monitored through the National Reporting Instrument, whose quantitative indicators have been NHWA indicators since 2017. About 15% of health and care workers globally work outside their country of birth or first qualification, varying by region and occupation; historic south-to-north patterns persist, but the line between source and destination countries is blurring. Global Strategy milestone 3 tracks progress towards halving reliance on foreign-trained professionals, and the density of selected workers, with the UHC service coverage index, determines inclusion on the WHO health workforce Support and Safeguards List. Suggested indicators: density of doctors, nurses, midwives, dentists and pharmacists (1-01, an SSL criterion), distribution by place of birth (1-07) and of training and country of training (1-08), inflows by place of training (1-09), and HRHIS ability to report on the Code and track entrants and exits (4-05.3, 4-05.5, 4-05.7).

sections.extract: The migration of HCWs is a policy question affecting most countries, either because of their reliance on foreign-trained HCWs or because a large proportion of their HWF emigrates. The WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel is monitored through the National Reporting Instrument (NRI). Since the launch of NHWA in 2017, quantitative indicators included in the NRI are part of

sections.title: Gender

summary.text: Gender section of Part IV, followed by the handbook's Glossary and References. The health and care sector is highly feminized — women are 67% of its wage workers — with marked occupational segregation by gender and women paid on average 76 cents per dollar paid to men; education can also produce gender imbalances. Suggested indicators: distribution by age and sex (1-03) and by sex (1-04), inflows (1-09) and outflows (1-10) by sex, applications, enrolments and graduates by sex (2-02 to 2-04), women in Ministry of Health leadership (4-03) and HRHIS ability to monitor the gender pay gap (4-05.9); a note explains that sex is the disaggregation used because information systems record it, but serves here as a proxy for gender as a social identity. The Glossary defines the terms the indicator sheets flag, among them accreditation, active health worker and the three activity levels (practising, professionally active, licensed to practise), age groups, CHWs, CPD, contract type, dual practice, the six System of Health Accounts facility types (HP.1–HP.6), SNA-based ownership types, gender (socially constructed) and sex (observed at birth), public and private education institutions (classed by management, not funding), the IHR, interprofessional education, job vacancy and vacancy rate, leadership role, place of birth and of training, the public health workforce, remuneration, social accountability, social determinants of health, status in employment, subnational level (first or second administrative level), and total expenditure on health workforce education, defined there as current and capital spending as a percentage of gross national income. The References list 115 numbered sources, chiefly WHO, World Health Assembly, ILO, OECD, UNESCO and UN documents and journal articles, mostly accessed July–August 2023.

sections.extract: One feature that characterizes the health and care sector in many countries is that it is a highly feminized sector. Across the world women represent 67% of wage workers in the health and care sector (103). One widespread feature of the health and care sector is a significant degree of occupational segregation by gender, both across health and care occupations and within them. sections.title: + Annex 1: Development of the NHWA and its revision

summary.text: Annex 1, Development of the NHWA and its revision: NHWA was launched as a data-sharing mechanism for Member States at the Fourth Global Forum on Human Resources for Health in Dublin in 2017, answering resolution WHA69.19's call for a core set of HRH data. For version 1, over 450 indicators gathered in October 2015 were filtered to 255, rated in a November 2015 Delphi consultation of over 70 experts on relevance, availability and use, and settled by a Technical Advisory Group in workshops at WHO headquarters; WHO also produced an implementation guide. Five years of implementation greatly increased country-validated workforce data and supported national labour market studies, while WHO documented feedback on feasibility and relevance through workshops, stakeholder meetings and roadmaps. A 2022 review found the implementation principles still valid and focused on streamlining indicators: the Health Workforce Department's data unit assessed reporting rates and proposed which indicators to keep, revise or reject; focal points in all six WHO regions and all regional offices responded to online surveys; WHO experts were interviewed; and a technical expert group, in a two-day workshop, recommended retaining, rejecting, modifying or merging indicators, adding new ones and improving implementation. NHWA will keep being reviewed and updated. The annex names version 1 contributors, the Technical Advisory Group, Delphi participants, and funders (the governments of Germany, Ireland, Japan and Norway and USAID).

It closes with three sources on classifying health workers, ISCO-08, and HRH monitoring and evaluation.
